failure_modes.description: Maximizing information flow correlates with maximizing traffic throughput
failure_modes.evidence: Information theory measures data correlation, not necessarily throughput. High mutual information could indicate congestion rather than efficiency. The fundamental assumption is untested and likely wrong.

failure_modes.description: Local measurements can estimate network-wide information flow
failure_modes.evidence: Network information theory shows that local measurements cannot reliably estimate global information flow without significant overhead. This contradicts established results in network information theory.

failure_modes.description: Information-theoretic optimization is computationally feasible in real-time
failure_modes.evidence: Calculating mutual information for even moderate-sized networks is NP-hard. Real-time traffic control requires millisecond decisions, making this approach computationally infeasible.
The predictions field is empty. Without specific, testable predictions, the hypothesis cannot be properly evaluated or falsified.
Information-theoretic approaches to traffic control have been explored since at least 2005 (e.g., work by Varaiya and others). The claimed novelty is overstated.

failure_modes.description: Self-organization conflicts with traffic safety requirements
failure_modes.evidence: Traffic systems must prioritize safety above all else. Purely information-theoretic optimization could create dangerous configurations that maximize information flow but violate safety constraints.

failure_modes.description: The network has sufficient heterogeneity to benefit from information maximization
failure_modes.evidence: Many real traffic networks have homogeneous sections where this approach would provide no benefit. The hypothesis doesn't address how to handle such cases.
